title: Quantifying the “infodemic”: People turned to trustworthy news outlets during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic
screen_reason: Behavioural trace study of an estimated 905B desktop and mobile visits to news websites (Comscore) and 54B Facebook engagements (CrowdTangle) generated by 3,592 NewsGuard-rated news outlets in the US, UK, France and Germany, 2017-2021. It reports, per country and year, the proportion of news web traffic captured by untrustworthy outlets (EXPOSURE, news-diet share) and the proportion of Facebook engagement with news outlets captured by them (SHARING, content share), each under two source-level definitions (NewsGuard score <= 60; outlet repeatedly publishes false content). All values are verbatim shares with stated denominators.

estimates.platform: news websites (desktop and mobile visits, Comscore)
estimates.measure_type: % of all visits to news websites in US that went to generally untrustworthy news outlets (NewsGuard score <= 60)
estimates.denominator: all visits to NewsGuard-rated news websites in US in 2020 (desktop + mobile, Comscore panel and census measurement; country-year totals are not printed - the four-country dataset covers an estimated 905B visits 2017-2021)
estimates.definition: Traffic/engagement attributed to an outlet with a NewsGuard trustworthiness score of 60 or lower ('generally untrustworthy').
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard categorizes news outlets with a score of 60 or lower as 'generally untrustworthy' and above 60 as 'generally trustworthy'"
estimates.n: all 2020 visits to news websites in US (Comscore panel N = 300K US / 55.5K UK / 23K France / 27K Germany plus census measurement)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard employs a team of journalists and editors who rate news outlets 0-100 on nine journalistic norms of credibility and transparency, including whether the outlet publishes false content and whether it uses deceptive headlines; 3,592 rated outlets across the four countries were used, platforms (e.g. YouTube) and satirical outlets (e.g. The Onion) excluded. Ratings are outlet-level, not article-level. The authors note the ratings resemble those of national fact-checkers ('Les Decodeurs', 'Media Bias Fact Check') and report robustness to using individual NewsGuard criteria separately.
estimates.moderator_quote: Comscore relies on panel (N = 300K in the US, 55.5K in the UK, 23K in France and 27K in Germany) and census measurement techniques to obtain longitudinal and cross-country unified digital audience measurement statistics. Comscore tracks desktop and mobile visits to news websites (on mobile it tracks visits via apps and mobile browsers).
estimates.notes: Coded EXPOSURE (diet_share) because the denominator is visits consumed, restricted to news websites - it is a share of the online NEWS diet, not of all web use. 2020 chosen as the representative time point (the pandemic year the paper is about); 2019 and pooled 2017-2021 values are in the same tables and are listed in missed_or_uncertain.

estimates.platform: Facebook (engagement on news outlets' Facebook pages, CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of all Facebook engagement with news outlets in US accumulated by generally untrustworthy news outlets (NewsGuard score <= 60)
estimates.denominator: all engagement (likes, emojis, shares, comments) on the posts of NewsGuard-rated news outlets' Facebook pages in US in 2020; country-year totals are not printed - the four-country dataset covers 54B Facebook engagements 2017-2021
estimates.definition: Traffic/engagement attributed to an outlet with a NewsGuard trustworthiness score of 60 or lower ('generally untrustworthy').
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard categorizes news outlets with a score of 60 or lower as 'generally untrustworthy' and above 60 as 'generally trustworthy'"
estimates.n: all 2020 Facebook engagements with news outlets' pages in US (~3,600 outlet pages covered across the four countries)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard employs a team of journalists and editors who rate news outlets 0-100 on nine journalistic norms of credibility and transparency, including whether the outlet publishes false content and whether it uses deceptive headlines; 3,592 rated outlets across the four countries were used, platforms (e.g. YouTube) and satirical outlets (e.g. The Onion) excluded. Ratings are outlet-level, not article-level. The authors note the ratings resemble those of national fact-checkers ('Les Decodeurs', 'Media Bias Fact Check') and report robustness to using individual NewsGuard criteria separately.
estimates.moderator_quote: Web traffic refers to the total number of visits to news websites, whereas Facebook engagement to the number of likes, emojis, shares, and comments, accumulated on the posts of news outlets' Facebook pages.
estimates.notes: Coded SHARING (content_share) because the denominator is engagement actions - likes, emojis, shares and comments - on outlets' posts, i.e. engagement rather than consumption; the schema has no dedicated 'engagement' unit, so unit='item' stands for engagement actions on news posts. The authors flag that CrowdTangle gives no impressions/reach and cannot see banned pages, which may understate engagement with misinformation. 2020 chosen as the representative time point (the pandemic year the paper is about); 2019 and pooled 2017-2021 values are in the same tables and are listed in missed_or_uncertain.

estimates.notes: Coded EXPOSURE (diet_share) because the denominator is visits consumed, restricted to news websites - it is a share of the online NEWS diet, not of all web use. definition_variant=true: stricter NewsGuard criterion (outlet repeatedly publishes false content) applied to the SAME country x platform cell as the 'generally untrustworthy' row, so the two are nested, not independent. GERMANY WEB CAVEAT: "As of September 2020, Comscore stopped tracking mobile web traffic in Germany. We excluded German data after August 2020", so the German 2020 web-traffic figure covers January-August 2020 only. 2020 chosen as the representative time point (the pandemic year the paper is about); 2019 and pooled 2017-2021 values are in the same tables and are listed in missed_or_uncertain.

estimates.platform: Facebook (engagement on news outlets' Facebook pages, CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of all Facebook engagement with news outlets in Germany accumulated by generally untrustworthy news outlets (NewsGuard score <= 60)
estimates.denominator: all engagement (likes, emojis, shares, comments) on the posts of NewsGuard-rated news outlets' Facebook pages in Germany in 2020; country-year totals are not printed - the four-country dataset covers 54B Facebook engagements 2017-2021
estimates.definition: Traffic/engagement attributed to an outlet with a NewsGuard trustworthiness score of 60 or lower ('generally untrustworthy').
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard categorizes news outlets with a score of 60 or lower as 'generally untrustworthy' and above 60 as 'generally trustworthy'"
estimates.n: all 2020 Facebook engagements with news outlets' pages in Germany (~3,600 outlet pages covered across the four countries)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard employs a team of journalists and editors who rate news outlets 0-100 on nine journalistic norms of credibility and transparency, including whether the outlet publishes false content and whether it uses deceptive headlines; 3,592 rated outlets across the four countries were used, platforms (e.g. YouTube) and satirical outlets (e.g. The Onion) excluded. Ratings are outlet-level, not article-level. The authors note the ratings resemble those of national fact-checkers ('Les Decodeurs', 'Media Bias Fact Check') and report robustness to using individual NewsGuard criteria separately.
estimates.moderator_quote: Web traffic refers to the total number of visits to news websites, whereas Facebook engagement to the number of likes, emojis, shares, and comments, accumulated on the posts of news outlets' Facebook pages.
estimates.notes: Coded SHARING (content_share) because the denominator is engagement actions - likes, emojis, shares and comments - on outlets' posts, i.e. engagement rather than consumption; the schema has no dedicated 'engagement' unit, so unit='item' stands for engagement actions on news posts. The authors flag that CrowdTangle gives no impressions/reach and cannot see banned pages, which may understate engagement with misinformation. 2020 chosen as the representative time point (the pandemic year the paper is about); 2019 and pooled 2017-2021 values are in the same tables and are listed in missed_or_uncertain.

estimates.platform: Facebook (engagement on news outlets' Facebook pages, CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of all Facebook engagement with news outlets in Germany accumulated by news outlets repeatedly publishing false content (NewsGuard)
estimates.denominator: all engagement (likes, emojis, shares, comments) on the posts of NewsGuard-rated news outlets' Facebook pages in Germany in 2020; country-year totals are not printed - the four-country dataset covers 54B Facebook engagements 2017-2021
estimates.definition: Traffic/engagement attributed to an outlet whose NewsGuard rating flags it as repeatedly publishing false content.
estimates.misinfo_def: "the subset of news outlets identified by NewsGuard as repeatedly publishing false content" (NewsGuard's individual 'Does not repeatedly publish false content' criterion)
estimates.n: all 2020 Facebook engagements with news outlets' pages in Germany (~3,600 outlet pages covered across the four countries)

missed_or_uncertain: (1) POOLED FOUR-COUNTRY VALUES NOT ENTERED AS ROWS, to avoid double-counting the same traffic already split by country: "In 2020, generally untrustworthy news outlets, as rated by NewsGuard, accounted for 2.28% of the web traffic to news outlets and 13.97% of the Facebook engagement with news outlets" and "In 2020, news outlets repeatedly publishing false content accounted for 1.39% of the web traffic to news outlets and 6.76% of the Facebook engagement with news outlets" (the abstract rounds these to 2.3%, 14.0%, 1.4% and 6.8%). If the review wants one row per study, use those four. (2) OTHER TIME POINTS AVAILABLE in Tables 2 and 3 but collapsed away per the time-series rule: untrustworthy web traffic 2019 US 3.22% / UK 0.13% / France 5.73% / Germany 0.93% and 2017-2021 US 3.36% / UK 0.10% / France 4.43% / Germany 0.97%; untrustworthy Facebook engagement 2019 US 17.42% / UK 3.11% / France 25.11% / Germany 7.45% and 2017-2021 US 18.52% / UK 2.44% / France 23.00% / Germany 8.52%; repeatedly-false web traffic 2019 US 0.94% / UK 0.025% / France 4.53% / Germany 0.91% and 2017-2021 US 0.97% / UK 0.018% / France 3.30% / Germany 0.96%; repeatedly-false Facebook engagement 2019 US 4.30% / UK 1.37% / France 15.78% / Germany 7.31% and 2017-2021 US 4.66% / UK 0.88% / France 13.35% / Germany 8.05%. (3) NOT EXTRACTED, not misinformation shares: year-on-year growth figures (web traffic +22.06% overall in 2020, +24.29% US, +24.58% UK, +26.00% France, +28.73% Germany; Facebook engagement +24.67% overall) and Table 6's growth-by-trustworthiness cells (e.g. untrustworthy web traffic +31.84% US, -10% UK ns, +0.12% France ns, +42% Germany); Table 5 Spearman correlations between trustworthiness and traffic; Table 4 per-outlet audience shares (e.g. BBC 30.6% of UK web traffic, Daily Mail 24.7% of UK Facebook engagement) - these are shares of traffic per OUTLET, not a top-X%-to-Y% concentration statistic, so no CONCENTRATION row is possible; page-like counts (1.2B trustworthy vs 213M untrustworthy pages). (4) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY for the adjudicator: the text says web traffic increased "26.00% in France (+ 3B)" while Table 6 gives France trustworthy web traffic as "+ 28% (3M)" - the units (3B vs 3M) and percentages disagree. Growth figures were not extracted, so no row is affected. (5) Estimates the paper quotes from other studies (Table 1: Grinberg 5%, Allen 1%, Guess 6%, Osmundsen 4%, Allen 2021 19.4%, Guess 2021 15%; and comparisons such as Boberg 1.1%, Marchal 4%) are citations to elsewhere and are excluded by R8. (6) Denominator caveat that limits interpretation: both measures are shares of NEWS only - news websites and news outlets' Facebook pages - not of all web browsing or of all Facebook content. The authors state that "news content represents a very small portion of posts on Facebook". Also source-level, not content-level: "our data speak to the misinformation debate at the source level (e.g. The New York Times), not at the content level". (7) Coverage caveat: NewsGuard rates many outlets that Comscore does not cover because they generate too little traffic, and CrowdTangle cannot see banned pages, so untrustworthy engagement may be understated.

rob.design: Cross-country, cross-platform observational trace study, July 2017 - July 2021. Web traffic: Comscore desktop + mobile visits to news websites, panel (N = 300,000 US; 55,500 UK; 23,000 France; 27,000 Germany) combined with census measurement; German data excluded after August 2020 because Comscore stopped tracking German mobile traffic. Facebook: CrowdTangle/Facebook API engagement (likes, emojis, shares, comments) on the main Facebook pages of the same outlets; pages not affiliated with the four countries excluded (national editions such as RT France/RT Germany kept). Source classification: NewsGuard ratings of 3,592 outlets, journalists scoring outlets 0-100 on nine credibility and transparency criteria, dichotomised at 60; platforms and satire excluded; no inter-rater reliability reported by the study (the rating instrument is external and proprietary). Analysis: random-effects within-between models on log-transformed traffic with year as within effect, trustworthiness and month as between effects, outlet random slopes; robustness to individual NewsGuard criteria, individual Facebook metrics, alternative Comscore metrics (unique visitors, total minutes) and to excluding large outlets (Fox News, CDC). Author-stated limits: no Facebook impressions or reach, banned pages invisible, volume does not capture distribution across the public, source-level not content-level, news-only denominators.
rob.item6_quote: NewsGuard employs a team of journalists and editors to rate news outlets from 0 to 100 based on nine journalistic norms of credibility and transparency, including whether they publish false content and/or use deceptive headlines ... NewsGuard categorizes news outlets with a score of 60 or lower as “generally untrustworthy” and above 60 as “generally trustworthy”.
